findings.claim: Three threads land cleanly on the technical-commercial intersection.
findings.failure_mode: count does not match enumeration
findings.evidence: The paragraph then lists five threads: Ch 6+8 liability/warranty, Ch 7-8 contracts, Ch 9 employment, Ch 12 FTC, Ch 2 TKI.
findings.fix: correct: Five threads land on the technical-commercial intersection.

findings.claim: GDPR/CCPA/COPPA are flagged in the source's Ch 12 framing of data privacy as code-of-conduct regulatory ethics
findings.failure_mode: source content invented; wrong chapter
findings.evidence: GDPR, CCPA and COPPA occur nowhere in the converted source or deep. Data privacy appears as a regulatory-ethics element of a code of conduct in Ch 3.1 (deep 158; source 1786), and as a Bureau of Consumer Protection remit in Ch 12.2 (deep 735).
findings.fix: correct: Data privacy appears only as a regulatory-ethics element of a code of conduct (Ch 3.1) and as a remit of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection (Ch 12.2); no data-protection regime (GDPR, CCPA, COPPA) is named. For data-protection compliance the practitioner needs counsel or a specialist reference outside this corpus.

findings.claim: The Chevron exemplar prices the savings empirically ($25,000 mediation vs $700,000 outside-legal vs $2.5M litigation).

findings.fix: correct: The Chevron exemplar illustrates the savings on one dispute ($25,000 via internal mediation vs an estimated $700,000 in outside legal services and $2.5M in court).

findings.claim: Software licences "have been treated variously as goods, mixed sales, and pure services"

findings.evidence: Deep 445 carries this unquoted as paraphrase. Source 4188-4190: 'Software licenses are not tangible, but they are also not movable, and have been treated in different ways: as goods, a mixed sale (a tangible item tied to an intangible item), and pure services.'
findings.fix: correct: Software licences have been treated variously as goods, mixed sales, and pure services (Ch 8.1, "The Uniform Commercial Code") — drop the quotation marks.

findings.claim: Special relationships (vendor-customer, employer-employee) imply elevated duties.
findings.failure_mode: examples not in source
findings.evidence: Deep 332 and source 3283-3287: a special relationship implies a duty to aid or protect, e.g. nurse to patient, lifeguard to swimmer. Vendor-customer and employer-employee are not named.
findings.fix: correct: Special relationships (e.g. nurse to patient, lifeguard to swimmer) imply a duty to aid or protect.

findings.claim: Foreseeability is the test that runs through both tort liability and contract anticipation.
findings.failure_mode: claim absent from deep and source
findings.evidence: Deep 334-336: foreseeability is a negligence concept (Ch 6.1). Neither deep nor source links foreseeability to contract law.
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: ADA: reasonable accommodation required absent undue burden; structured interactive review. ... (Source: Ch 9.1)
findings.failure_mode: procedure not in source; ADA mis-cited to Ch 9.1
findings.evidence: Deep 642 (Ch 9.3): ADA requires reasonable accommodations not imposing undue burden; three plaintiff requirements. No 'interactive' process anywhere in the source. ADA is Ch 9.3, FMLA Ch 9.1. The same premise recurs in the Phase 3 question at line 80.
findings.fix: correct: ADA: reasonable accommodation required unless it imposes an undue burden; a plaintiff must show a disability, an adverse decision because of it, and that they were otherwise qualified. (Source: Ch 9.1 for FMLA; Ch 9.3 for ADA)

findings.claim: Software marketing claims, dark-pattern UX, hidden subscription terms, and AI-capability puffery cross into this regime.
findings.failure_mode: puffery placed inside FTC prohibition; source treats puffery as lawful
findings.evidence: Deep 498 / source 4470-4474: 'Puffery, or language used to bolster sales, is lawful'. Deep 714: deceptive practices are misrepresentations that are substantial. Same premise at line 62 ('FTC scrutiny on AI puffery').
findings.fix: correct: Software marketing claims, hidden subscription terms, and AI-capability claims that misrepresent the product cross into this regime; obvious sales talk (puffery) is lawful (Ch 8.2).

findings.claim: Sherman Act (... price-fixing, market-allocation agreements)
findings.failure_mode: in source but not in deep
findings.evidence: Deep 691 carries only 'agreements with competitors to set prices'. Source 5918-5920: 'agreements to fix prices or bids or allocate customers are considered criminal felonies'.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep 691: 'Mergers or other actions that would create agreements to fix prices or bids or allocate customers are considered criminal felonies' [V] (Ch 11.2, "Antitrust Laws").

findings.claim: Is the worker actually a contractor (control, equipment, schedule autonomy, multiple clients) or an employee misclassified? Wage-hour, FLSA, workers' comp, FMLA, and tax consequences follow.
findings.failure_mode: legal test and consequences not in source

findings.claim: Foreseeability is the test that runs through both tort liability and contract anticipation.
findings.failure_mode: claim absent from deep and source
findings.evidence: As S009: foreseeability is Ch 6.1 negligence only (deep 334-336).
findings.fix: correct: Was the harm reasonably foreseeable? Foreseeability is central to negligence (Ch 6.1, "Foreseeability").

findings.claim: Surface Schedule 13D / Form 8-K disclosure trigger ... does this incident trigger 8-K disclosure ... Is the materiality threshold met for insider-trading silence obligations?
findings.failure_mode: Schedule 13D misapplied to incident disclosure
findings.evidence: Deep 842: Schedule 13D is filed within 10 days by anyone becoming beneficial owner of more than 5% of a company's stock; it has nothing to do with incidents. Deep 850: 8-K triggers named are officer changes, mergers, bankruptcy.
findings.fix: correct: Surface Form 8-K disclosure trigger | If we are publicly held, does this event require a Form 8-K (filed within four business days; named triggers include officer changes, mergers, bankruptcy)? Are insiders barred from trading on it as material nonpublic information?

findings.claim: trade-secret status requires reasonable measures to maintain secrecy
findings.failure_mode: legal rule not in source
findings.evidence: Trade secrets appear only as an example of IP in arbitration property disputes (deep 106; source 1259). No rule on maintaining trade-secret status.
findings.fix: strip the parenthetical

findings.claim: Hiding foreseeable risk creates governance liability beyond the operational risk itself.
findings.failure_mode: legal claim not in source
findings.evidence: No governance-liability rule for board reporting in deep or source; foreseeability is a negligence concept (deep 334-336).
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: false endorsements ("our security team is the best in the industry")
findings.failure_mode: concept mislabelled
findings.evidence: Deep 720: false endorsements = fabricated testimonials. A 'best in the industry' self-claim matches the source's example of lawful puffery ('this sandwich is the best in the world', deep 498).
findings.fix: correct: specific guarantees ("this will never happen again"), fabricated testimonials, or hidden remedy conditions

findings.claim: claims have crossed from puffery into express warranty under UCC 8.2
findings.failure_mode: book section cited as a UCC section
findings.evidence: 8.2 is the book's section ('Warranties and Sales Contracts'); UCC sections in the deep are numbered 1-203, 2-105, 2-205, 2-305 etc. Same mis-cite at lines 58 ('UCC 8.2') and 163 ('UCC 8.2 applies').
findings.fix: correct: ... into express warranty (Ch 8.2, "Express and Implied Warranties")

findings.claim: voluntary compliance through consent order may produce better long-term outcomes; regulators are stakeholders, not adversaries. Follow-up: evaluate negotiation, then mediation, then formal proceedings; the Chevron cost arithmetic generalises to regulatory contexts.
findings.failure_mode: outcome claim and generalisation not in source
findings.evidence: Deep 737-741 lists consent order as one FTC recourse option, with no outcome comparison. Chevron (deep 71, [AE]) is one internal commercial dispute; nothing extends it to regulators.
findings.fix: correct: Diagnosis: the FTC's recourse options include voluntary compliance through a consent order as well as administrative complaints and federal litigation (Ch 12.2). Follow-up: evaluate the consent-order route before defaulting to litigation.

findings.claim: the six named categories include misrepresenting a product and giving false impressions
findings.failure_mode: invented category
findings.evidence: Deep 718-725: the six categories are product guarantees and false endorsements; unfair advertising; taking advantage of customers; misrepresenting a product; giving misleading price information; failing to disclose pertinent information. 'Giving false impressions' is not one.
findings.fix: correct: the six named categories include misrepresenting a product and failing to disclose pertinent information

findings.claim: Title VII disparate-impact analysis applies not only to direct employers but to software products that function as hiring filters — the Griggs two-route framework (disparate treatment and disparate impact) is the operative test
findings.failure_mode: legal reach not in source; Griggs mis-described
findings.evidence: Deep 616: Title VII covers commercial employers with 15+ employees; nothing extends it to vendors of screening software. Deep 619 / source 5122-5132: Griggs is the disparate-impact exemplar and established the disparate-impact steps, not a two-route framework.
findings.fix: correct: Title VII disparate-impact analysis applies to the customers who use the screening output in hiring (employers with 15+ employees); Griggs is the source's disparate-impact exemplar (Ch 9.3, "Civil Rights Act of 1964 – Title VII").

findings.claim: the "fairness-tested" claim has moved from puffery into an express warranty under UCC Article 2
findings.failure_mode: applies Article 2 to a SaaS product without the goods caveat
findings.evidence: Deep 445: Article 2 governs sales of goods; software licences have been treated variously as goods, mixed sales, and pure services. The distillation's own KC7 (line 28) says to treat this as unresolved.
findings.fix: correct: the "fairness-tested" claim reads as a specific assertion of fact rather than sales talk; if the product is treated as goods under UCC Article 2, it becomes an express warranty (Ch 8.1, 8.2).

findings.claim: Section names cited: "The FTC and Unfair Trade Practices", "Title VII of the Civil Rights Act", "Sales Warranties" (lines 150, 156, 191), "Tort Law — Negligence" and "Contract Remedies" (line 152)
findings.failure_mode: section names that do not exist in source or deep
findings.evidence: Source headings: 'Unfair Trade Practices and Examples' (6210), 'Civil Rights Act of 1964 – Title VII' (5082), 'Warranties' / 'Express and Implied Warranties' (4407/4424), 'Negligence' (3257), 'Remedies' (3924).
findings.fix: correct: use (Ch 12.1, "Unfair Trade Practices and Examples"); (Ch 9.3, "Civil Rights Act of 1964 – Title VII"); (Ch 8.2, "Express and Implied Warranties"); (Ch 6.1, "Negligence"); (Ch 7.3, "Remedies")

findings.claim: foreseeability runs through both tort and contract ... (Source: Ch 6.1 ...; Ch 7.3, "Contract Remedies")
findings.failure_mode: claim absent from deep and source; Ch 7.3 cited for it
findings.evidence: Deep 406-420 (Ch 7.3) covers breach and remedies with no foreseeability; foreseeability is Ch 6.1 only (deep 334-336).
findings.fix: correct: The reasonable-person standard and the foreseeability test govern the negligence surface (Ch 6.1, "Negligence"; "Foreseeability"): the company can foresee that customers will use the output in adverse employment decisions.

findings.claim: the "fairness-tested" claim fails the reasonableness-of-reliance test given the documented gap — the claim has crossed into express warranty and a disclaimer does not cure its centre of gravity
findings.failure_mode: concept misapplied; disclaimer rule not in source
findings.evidence: Deep 498 / source 4468-4474: the reasonableness test of reliance separates statements a buyer may rely on (warranty) from sales talk (puffery). A claim that 'fails' the test would be puffery, not a warranty. The source says nothing about disclaimers.
findings.fix: correct: the general counsel concludes that a customer could reasonably rely on "fairness-tested" as a statement of fact, so it would operate as an express warranty that the documented gap would breach (Ch 8.2).

findings.claim: allocate disparate-impact-analysis responsibility explicitly in the customer ToS, which UCC permits between sophisticated commercial parties
findings.failure_mode: legal permission not in source
findings.evidence: Nothing in deep Ch 8 (422-520) or Ch 12 on allocating Title VII analysis by contract or on 'sophisticated commercial parties'.
findings.fix: correct: ... document the gap transparently for customer HR functions and state in the customer ToS that customers remain responsible for their own disparate-impact analysis.

findings.claim: Copyright (most software protection), patent (algorithmic claims), trade-secret (kept-secret algorithms and process), and trademark (brand) carry distinct rules ... The source surveys this at Ch 1.3
findings.failure_mode: IP doctrine not in source; survey claim false
findings.evidence: Copyright is not mentioned anywhere in the source. IP appears only as a list item at Ch 1.3 (source 577), as a property-dispute category for arbitration (Ch 2.3, deep 106) and in the warranty against infringement (Ch 8.2, deep 502).
findings.fix: correct: Treating IP exposure as legal-team-only in build-vs-buy. The source only names IP (Ch 1.3 list; Ch 2.3 arbitration of trade secrets, inventions, artistic works; Ch 8.2 implied warranty against infringement); IP doctrine needs a specialist reference.

findings.claim: Unconstitutional under the Thirteenth Amendment as forced labour. Money damages or substitute performance is the only remedy
findings.failure_mode: amendment not named in source; remedy set narrowed
findings.evidence: Deep 420: 'forced labor, i.e. slavery, which is in violation of the U.S. Constitution' — no amendment named; 'Thirteenth' absent from source. Deep 414-420 lists five remedies (money damages, restitution, rescission, reformation, specific performance), so money damages is not the only one left.
findings.fix: correct: Compelling personal service 'would constitute forced labor, i.e. slavery, which is in violation of the U.S. Constitution' [V] (Ch 7.3). Money damages, restitution or rescission remain available.

findings.claim: long-term reputation cost typically exceeds short-term litigation-avoidance benefit

findings.claim: Voluntary compliance through consent order produces better long-term outcomes than litigation. Regulators are stakeholders.
findings.failure_mode: outcome claim not in source
findings.evidence: Deep 737-741 lists consent order as one FTC recourse option with no comparison of outcomes.
findings.fix: correct: Treating regulators as adversaries by default. The FTC's recourse options include voluntary compliance through a consent order before administrative complaints or federal litigation (Ch 12.2).

findings.claim: Hiding material undisclosed events to manage news cycle. 8-K disclosure within 4 business days; Schedule 13D within 10 days; ... Hiding the event compounds the underlying problem with disclosure liability.
findings.failure_mode: Schedule 13D misapplied; liability claim not in source
findings.evidence: Deep 842: Schedule 13D is a >5% beneficial-ownership filing, not an event disclosure. Figures (4 business days, 10 days) are correct. No disclosure-liability statement in deep.
findings.fix: correct: Delaying required event disclosure. Events such as officer changes, mergers or bankruptcy require a Form 8-K within four business days (Ch 14.1), and insiders may not trade on material nonpublic information meanwhile.

findings.claim: Misclassifying employees as contractors ... FLSA, FMLA, workers' comp, tax, and Title VII obligations follow actual relationship, not contractual label. Liability accumulates silently until it surfaces.
findings.failure_mode: doctrine not in source

findings.claim: NHS Just Culture's default-to-system framing ... complements Business Law's foreseeability-and-reasonable-person standard for negligence. Both refuse pure individual-blame as the explanation for system failure.
findings.failure_mode: position attributed to Business Law that its deep does not hold
findings.evidence: NHS deep 15/42 supports the default-to-system prior. Business-law deep 302: tort law addresses damage 'based on fault'; the reasonable-person standard (332) judges an individual's conduct. Nothing in Business Law refuses individual blame.
findings.fix: correct: NHS Just Culture's foresight test (Q3) and Business Law's foreseeability test for negligence (Ch 6.1) both ask whether harm could reasonably have been foreseen; NHS then defaults to system causes, while tort law assigns fault to the party that breached a duty.

findings.claim: The Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument (TKI) is attributed to Pruitt and Rubin as borrowed-through lineage
findings.failure_mode: misattribution
findings.evidence: Deep 53: the TKI 'is closely associated with work done by conflict resolution experts Dean Pruitt and Jeffrey Rubin'; deep 911: Kilmann and Thomas (1977) is the instrument's endnote citation.
findings.fix: correct: The Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument (Kilmann and Thomas, 1977) is described as closely associated with the work of Pruitt and Rubin; neither is held independently.

findings.claim: The Griggs ... statistical examples ... are from the case itself, cited as [BT] in the deep reference (repeated at line 193: 'Claims attributed to the TKI instrument and the Griggs statistical examples are [BT] in the deep ref')

findings.fix: correct: The Griggs figures are carried as [V] in the deep reference (the source's own statement of the case facts); the case record is not held.

findings.claim: The Chevron mediation cost-savings data is cited from Chevron's own reported programme

findings.evidence: Source 1043-1047 states the Chevron figures with no citation or data source; deep 71 marks the example [AE].
findings.fix: correct: The Chevron mediation figures are given by the source without a cited origin; treat them as an [AE] example.

findings.claim: it explicitly covers American legal doctrine and does not develop non-US regimes

findings.evidence: Deep 745-806 (Ch 13) and 490-492 (Ch 8.1) cover international law, the CISG, the UN and EU, comity, act of state and common vs civil law systems.

findings.claim: GDPR, CCPA, and COPPA appear only as regulatory-ethics flags in Ch 12's framing of data privacy as code-of-conduct obligations
findings.failure_mode: source content invented; wrong chapter
findings.evidence: As S002: none of the three is mentioned in the source; the code-of-conduct data-privacy mention is Ch 3.1 (source 1786, deep 158).
findings.fix: correct: No data-protection regime (GDPR, CCPA, COPPA) is named; data privacy appears only as a code-of-conduct example (Ch 3.1) and an FTC Bureau of Consumer Protection remit (Ch 12.2).

findings.claim: The Lanham Act, patent, copyright, and trade-secret material is surveyed at Ch 1.3 and appears in Ch 8 in the warranty-against-infringement context
findings.failure_mode: coverage overstated
findings.evidence: The Lanham Act and copyright are not mentioned in the source. Ch 1.3 only lists 'intellectual property' among business-law disciplines (source 577); trade secrets appear in Ch 2.3 (source 1259); Ch 8.2 names trademark and patent infringement (source 4494).
findings.fix: correct: IP is only named: in the Ch 1.3 list of business-law disciplines, in Ch 2.3 (trade secrets, inventions and artistic works as arbitration subjects) and in the Ch 8.2 implied warranty against infringement. The Lanham Act and copyright are not mentioned.

findings.claim: The source's own structure note reads: "a brief introductory text that covers key concepts necessary to establish a strong foundation in the subject."
findings.failure_mode: deep paraphrase quoted as source words
findings.evidence: Deep 7 quotes only 'key concepts necessary to establish a strong foundation in the subject'. Source 317-319: 'a brief introductory textbook designed to meet the scope and sequence requirements ... cover the key concepts necessary to establish a strong foundation in the subject.'
findings.fix: correct: The preface describes it as "a brief introductory textbook" whose concepts "cover the key concepts necessary to establish a strong foundation in the subject" [V] (Preface, "About Business Law I Essentials").

notes: Heaviest drift of the three distillations: much of the software-specific layer (IP regimes, contractor misclassification, ADA interactive process, trade-secret maintenance, consent-order outcomes, Title VII reach to software vendors) is outside-the-source legal knowledge dressed in source citations. Foreseeability-in-contract appears three times (S009, S014, S025). All [V] quotes match the converted source; one re-extracted (S005), two non-verbatim quoted passages (S007, S044). Worked example carries no verbatim blockquote (protocol asks for one); not graded. Integration rows on jones-evidence-based-sweng, openstax-accounting-vol2 and openstax-principles-marketing check against their deep refs. The integration rows to sibling distillations (decision-making, stakeholder-engagement) describe those files accurately.
